subject: mathematics
question_text: If A + B + C = 2S, then prove that sin(S−A) + sin(S−B) + sinC = 4 cos((S−A)/2) cos((S−B)/2) sin(C/2).

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.42 — LAQ chapter 5 T-Ratios upto Transformations, answer 30.1. Printed appearances: TS 16. The S-family. The condition is A + B + C = 2S, so (A+B) + C = 2S and (S−A) + (S−B) = 2S − (A+B) = C — the substitution every step below turns on. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed anywhere in this chapter (its pages are set two questions to a page in two columns, which takes the margin those tags would occupy). The 1+2+2+1+1 above follows the shape of the split the same book DOES print for LAQ answer 23 on book p.37, weighting the two substantial transformations against the set-up and the finish. The SAME split and the SAME step ids are used on all eight answers in this chapter, deliberately: they are ONE method over different identities — pair two terms, use the angle condition, factor, finish with a product formula. A student who learns that arc once can attempt any of them. The book's chapter header carries ★★ and reads '7 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q23 is the Transformations slot and is ALWAYS a question of this kind. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark, and the key observation: the two shifted angles ADD to C. Work that out before starting or none of the substitutions below will be visible.
steps.memory_tip: The key observation: the two shifted angles ADD to C. Nothing below is visible without it.

recall.must_convey: That the angle condition is written down first, in the form the proof will actually use.
accept: write the angle condition first in the form the proof needs
state the given condition and rearrange it
note the angle sum before starting the transformation
modata angle condition rasi, kavalsina form lo pettali
write down the condition on the angles

steps.why: Without the condition the statement is simply false, so it is not preamble — it is the hypothesis the whole proof uses, and it is used at least twice below.
common_mistakes: Starting the transformation before writing the condition.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. Three terms will not factorise as they stand, so two of them are combined into a product first. Quote the formula in brackets — the formulas are what the examiner marks.
steps.memory_tip: Pair the two S-terms together, not one of them with sin C. The half-difference is (B−A)/2.

recall.must_convey: That the first two terms are paired with the sin C + sin D formula, giving a half-sum of 2S − (A+B) and a half-difference of (B−A)/2.
accept: pair the first two with sin C plus sin D, the half sum is two S minus A plus B over two
apply sum to product to the two shifted terms
combine sin S minus A and sin S minus B
modati rendu ni sum to product cheyyali
use the sine sum formula on the first pair

steps.why: The two S-terms differ only in which of A and B is subtracted, so their sum and difference are both simple — which is exactly what the formula needs.
common_mistakes: Pairing one S-term with sin C instead.
Getting the half-difference as (A−B)/2 and picking up a sign.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. This is where the angle condition is used: it converts an expression in A and B into one in C, so that every term shares a factor.
steps.memory_tip: Expand sin C too, and note 2S − (A+B) is exactly C.

recall.must_convey: That 2S − (A+B) is replaced by C so the half-sum becomes C/2, and that sin C is expanded as 2 sin(C/2) cos(C/2) so both terms share sin(C/2).
accept: two S minus A plus B is C so the half sum is C over two, and expand sin C as two sin half C cos half C
use the condition to get C over two and expand the last sine
both terms now carry sin C over two
two S minus A plus B ante C, so C by two vasthundi
substitute and expand so both terms share a factor

steps.why: Expanding sin C into half angles is what lets the third term join the other two. Without it there is no common factor to take out.
common_mistakes: Substituting 2S − (A+B) as something other than C.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. The common factor comes out, and the condition is used a SECOND time inside the bracket so that both bracket terms are the same kind of function.
steps.memory_tip: The common factor comes out, and the condition is used again inside the bracket.

recall.must_convey: That 2 sin(C/2) is taken out and cos(C/2) rewritten using C = (S−A) + (S−B), so both bracket terms are in the shifted angles.
accept: take two sin C over two common then write C over two back in terms of S minus A and S minus B
factor out and convert the cosine back to the shifted angles
the bracket becomes two cosines in S minus A and S minus B
two sin C by two common teesi, C ni S minus A plus S minus B ga marchali
rewrite so the bracket is in the shifted angles

steps.why: The condition is used a second time, in reverse — C back into (S−A) + (S−B) — because the answer is stated in those shifted angles, not in C.
common_mistakes: Leaving the bracket in terms of C and B − A, which cannot combine.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One more sum-or-difference formula turns the bracket into a product, and the identity is complete. Write "= R.H.S" so the examiner can see the proof finished.
steps.memory_tip: One more formula turns the bracket into a product, giving the 4 in the answer.

recall.must_convey: That the sum of cosines becomes 2 cos((S−A)/2) cos((S−B)/2), giving 4 cos((S−A)/2) cos((S−B)/2) sin(C/2).
accept: the sum of cosines gives two cos S minus A over two cos S minus B over two so the answer is four of those times sin half C
apply the cosine sum formula to finish
the bracket becomes two cos half S minus A cos half S minus B
cos sum formula tho answer vasthundi, four cos cos sin
the final answer is four cos half S minus A cos half S minus B sin half C

steps.why: The 2 outside and the 2 from the formula multiply to the 4 in the answer.
common_mistakes: Getting the arguments of the two cosines swapped.

insider_note: The condition gives (S−A) + (S−B) = C, replacing the usual 180° step. There is no −1 in this answer, because sinC = 2sin(C/2)cos(C/2) needs no constant term.
